full_judgment:
2.The case against the petitioners under sections 304, 426, 380, 379 and 148 B. P. C. started on the complaint of opposite party No. 2. It was alleged that the petitioners who had litigation with the complainant party having been unsuccessful in obtaining a decree against the latter and taking advantage of the disturbed situation during the occupation period looted away their movable properties and after a few days caused multiple grievous injuries on Bisweswar Chakrabarty, brother of the complainant-opposite party No. 2 as a result of which he died after 8 days. 

 3. On an application of the opposite-party No.2 the learned Sessions Judge however cancelled the bail of the petitioners on 16.11.73. After a lapse of a month from this date the petitioners surrendered before the Court on 21.12.73 the date fixed for evidence when they were taken into custody. Six witnesses including the complainant opposite party No. 2 were examined on that date and 22.1.74 was fixed for examination of the remaining witnesses. On the same date, i.e., 21.12.73, the petitioners move the learned Magistrate for bail on the ground that the learned Sessions Judge had cancelled their bail but nonetheless, as the evidence of the prosecution witnesses who were examined on the date, did not establish any prima facie case against them they were entitled to bail. Their application for bail was heard by the learned Magistrate on 22.12.73. By his order dated 24.12.73 the Magistrate granted bail to the Petitioners under section 497(2) Cr. P. C. It is as follows 

 “…………………..On 24.12.73, the learned Lower Court granted bail to all the accused persons in defiance of my aforesaid order dated 16.11.73 passed in Criminal Misc. Case No. 231 of 1973. It appears to be a clear case of contempt by the Lower Court in defiance of the order of the Superior Court. 

 However, no new point was raised before me besides what was submitted before me in Criminal Misc. Case No. 231 of 1973. The bail is cancelled and the learned Lower Court should take all the accused 0. P.s to custody and report compliance at an early date. Copy to the Magistrate for information and guidance. The prayer for cancellation of bail is thus accepted. 

 Since I have already held that there has of contempt by the Magistrate concerned, start a Misc. Judi. case against the Magistrate (Mr. Md. K. Hossein) and the conducting Mukhtear ( Mr. Md Afsar Ali Mia) for the alleged offence of contempt of Court. In the meantime stay further proceeding of G. R. R. No. 564 of 1972 till the disposal of the contempt proceeding. 

 “If it appears to such officer or Court at any stage of the investigation",  inquiry or trail the case may be that there are not reasonable ground for believing that the accused  has  committed (a non-bailable offence) but that  there are sufficient grounds for further  inquiry into his guilt, the accused shall pending such inquiry be released on bail or at the discretion of such officer on the execution by him of a bond without sureties for his appearance as hereafter provided." 

 The learned Advocate referred to the interpretation put upon the scope and meaning of the provisions of the aforesaid section in the case of Bhore Singh and ors. Vs. State, A.I.R. 1956 (Allahabad) 671 and in the case of Abdul Hayee Khan Vs. The State, 10 D.L.R. (S.C.) 179. 

 8. In the first case the question was whether, if once bail has been refused by the Sessions Judge during enquiry stage, it is open to the Magistrate before whom the enquriy is pending to grant bail ? Mehrotra, J. who delivered the judgment was of the opinion that there is nothing in the Code of Criminal Procedure which bars a Magistrate from granting bail even though bail may have been refused by the Sessions Judge at an earlier stage. He observed : 

 9. In the second of the above mentioned cases the facts were that an Additional Magistrate before whom the accused who was arrested on a charge under section 436 P.P.C. was produced granted bail to him. This order was set aside by the Sessions Judge. An application Which was moved before the High Court against order of cancellation of bail was dismissed by a short order as follows :- 

 After this order was passed the case was entrusted to another Magistrate for trial who twice granted bail to the accused but twice the bail was cancelled by the learned Sessions Judge, on the ground that the Magistrate had no power to grant bail without complying with the order of the High Court. Subsequently a proceeding for contempt against the Magistrate was initiated by the complainant before the High Court. The High Court accepted the above-mentioned interpretation of the previous order in which it kept the question of bail for the decision of the Magistrate after some evidence was recorded. On appeal whether the views as expressed by the learned Sessions Judge or the High Court were valid. Cornelius, J. as he was then has repudiated the views of the High Court and observed as follows :- 

 "Viewing the case as a whole from its commencement with a much delayed initial report up to its conclusion on a discharge order which was left unchallenged, It clearly emerges that the only obstacle in the way of the grant of bail by the trial Magistrate was thought to lie in the wording of the order made in the High Court on the 23rd July 1954. That order which merely said that the question of bail was left to be decided by the trial Magistrate after some evidence was recorded has been interpreted by the Sessions Judge and in the High Court as if it was the source of power in the Magistrate in regard to the grant of bail. That view is plainly fallacious for, the Magistrate derived his power of granting ball from section 497 of the Criminal P.C. and no restraints upon that power can be recognized except such as appear in the section itself. The present was clearly a case in which bail could have been granted by the Magistrate provided he was satisfied that there was no reasonable ground for thinking that the offence lay under section 436 P.P.C. and for this purpose it was not a necessary condition that any evidence should have been recorded in the case." 

 10. In the present case it appears that as soon as the learned Sessions Judge came to learn that in spite of his order  cancelling the bail the Magistrate had again granted bail to the petitioners he took it more as an affront to his own order than considered its legality. He did not consider whether the Magistrate had any power to grant bail in the circumstances as he did irrespective of the fact that he had earlier cancelled the bail. Leaving aside the failure of the learned Sessions Judge to take into consideration whether the Magistrate had properly exercised the power to grant bail which he has under the provisions of section 497 (2) Cr. P C for if such failure other than the propriety of the Magistrate's order was only involved, he would have in following the case reported in 10 D.L.R. (S.C) 179 set aside the order of the Sessions Judge but since the propriety of the Magistrate's Order against the background mentioned above has been the subject of vehement criticism by Mr. Abdur Rasheed, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No.2, we may proceed to consider the same. He pointed out that when it was prayed on behalf of the prosecution that five witnesses have been gained over and there were other  material witnesses, the learned Magistrate ought not to have granted bail before their examination. Keeping in view the facts and circumstances leading to the order by which the Magistrate granted, bail to the petitioners it appears that if the Magistrate would have waited till the examination of some material witnesses as prayed for by the prosecution and then arrived at the conclusion to grant bail to the petitioners, his order, it could have been said, has satisfied the appearance or justice and also that it did not suffer from any lack of property. The learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 2 cited the case of Nadara Vs Jamait Khan 20 D.L.R. (S.C.) 245 and relied upon the following observations of Muhammad Yaqub Ali, J — 

 " ...After the material witnesses in the case have been examined the Sessions Judge or the High Court if satisfied that reasonable grounds do not appear for be-living that the accused has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or transportation for life may grant bail to him." 

 11.Having regard to the principles enunciated in the case referred to above a Magistrate when he grants bail to the accused or refutes to grant it derives his power to do go from the provisions of section 497(2) Cr. P.C. We cannot therefore approve the reasoning of the learned Sessions Judge in condemning the order or the Magistrate. The question which arises for determination being pot so much whether the Magistrate had power to grant bail in view of the order of cancellation of hail by the Session Judge but whether he should have granted bail to the petitioners before the conclusion of the enquiry or the examination of at least a few material witnesses we are in taking this aspect of the case into consideration unable to uphold his order. It lacks propriety both because it is tainted with hastiness that is undue and because it does not satisfy the appearance of justice which is better felt than expressed. 

 12. In these circumstances we uphold the order of the learned Sessions Judge but as already mentioned not on the ground stated by him in his order. The learned Magistrate will, however, be at liberty to consider the question of bail on the conclusion of the enquiry or on the examination of at least some of the material witnesses in this case. 

 Let the records of the case be sent down at once for proceeding with the case expeditiously.
